note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: You've seen that the single owner decides who destroys a value.
Now: exactly when that happens, in what order, and why Rust still lets you skip it.
Here is a pipeline stage. It reads a flag under a reader-writer lock, and if the flag isn't set, it takes the write lock and sets it.
It's the Rust Edition Guide's own example.
Compiled with the twenty twenty-one edition, it hangs forever. Compiled with the twenty twenty-four edition, it runs.
Same source. The only thing that changed is when a temporary dies.
By the end, you'll place every destructor in a program on a timeline, build a wrapper that closes a file exactly once, and know why leaking is allowed.
When a value is no longer needed, Rust runs its destructor.
And a destructor is two parts.
First, your drop, if the type has one. Then the compiler's own drop glue, which drops every field... in the order you wrote them.
So this stage logs its own name first, then name, input, and the spill file.
Most types never write a drop at all. The glue already drops their fields.
Our probe, a trace, is just a value whose drop writes its name to a log.
Let's predict one.
Three locals, declared in order: a, then b, then c.
At the closing brace, in what order do they die?
answer: The reverse. C, then b, then a.
That's the opposite of struct fields... and there's a reason. A later local may be borrowing an earlier one, so it has to go first.

lines: Where does a value die? Where its last owner ends.
After a move, the owner is the new binding. So m dies at the closing brace of the function it was handed to, and the brace in main drops nothing for it.
Mem drop isn't magic. It's a function that takes ownership and returns, so the value dies right there.
On a copy type, it does nothing... the original stays.
And assigning over a variable drops the old value on the spot.
Your type has a drop. You hold x, and you write x dot drop.
Does the compiler let you run the destructor by hand?
answer: Rejected. The explicit destructor call error.
Your call would run drop, and then the brace would run it again... so Rust forbids the call, and offers mem drop instead.

lines: Why can't a file handle be copy?
Because two copies would close the same file twice.
A type with a drop manages something besides its own bytes, so a bitwise copy would duplicate that responsibility.
That's why copy and drop never meet. The compiler rejects it.
Put three rules together. One owner. A move empties the source. And no copy on a type with a destructor.
Exactly once isn't a convention... it's a theorem.
Now the real thing. A spill file: a temporary file that's closed and unlinked in drop.
RAII in Rust is just ownership plus drop.
Hand it through two functions and back... one close, one unlink.
No defer. No finally. No with. There is exactly one owner, and its scope end is the release.
The file itself is four bytes, the descriptor.
One caveat: errors on close are ignored by drop. Call sync all first, if they matter.
A spool owns a directory guard and a file guard, in that order.
The directory's drop removes the directory. The file's drop removes the file.
After the spool is dropped, what's left on disk?
answer: The directory stays.
Dir is declared first, so it drops first, while the file is still inside... and removing a full directory fails.
Declare the spill file first, and both go.

lines: A temporary is a value with no name.
It dies at the semicolon. That lock guard is gone before the next statement.
Unless a let borrows it... then it lives to the end of the block.
And a match scrutinee's temporaries live through every arm.
That's how a lock gets held longer than it looks.
Back to the stage under the old edition. The migration lint fires.
You run the automatic fix.
What does it produce... and is the deadlock gone?
answer: It rewrites the if let into a match... and the match keeps the old order. The deadlock stays.
The guide says: review each rewrite, and put the if let back where you want the shorter life.

lines: Rust twenty twenty-four changes two temporary scopes. Both make a temporary die sooner.
In an if let, the scrutinee's temporaries now drop before the else branch.
In a block's tail expression, they drop before the block's own locals.
That one badge, landing on the other side of the else, is the whole difference between hanging and running.
A match is unchanged.
The Edition Guide's other example. A function ends with a borrow of a ref cell, as its tail expression.
Which editions compile it?
answer: Only twenty twenty-four.
In the old edition, the borrow guard outlived the cell itself, so the compiler refused... the does-not-live-long-enough error.
Now the guard goes first, and it compiles.

lines: Here's a value moved on one path only.
So at the closing brace, who knows whether to drop it?
Only the running program does. So the compiler keeps a one-bit flag on the stack, and checks it at the brace.
You can see it in the compiler's intermediate code: a constant true, a constant false, and a switch.
Destructors run on the normal path. And a panic still drops everything on its way out, in the same reverse order.
But process exit drops nothing.
And with panic set to abort, nothing either.
So a spill file is cleaned up after a panic, but not after an exit.
One more rule: a drop that panics while already unwinding aborts the whole process. Keep drop bodies simple.
Mem forget takes a value and never drops it.
The file stays open, and on disk. The path's buffer is never freed... the counting allocator sees one allocation too many.
And all of that is safe code.
Because Rust never promised destructors would run.
Leaking is usually a bug. But it's a memory-safe bug.
Four ways to end up with a value that never drops.
Which of them needs unsafe?
answer: None of them. Leaking is safe... forget, box leak, a reference-count cycle, process exit.
The unsafe one is running a destructor by hand, with manually drop's drop, because nothing stops it running twice.

lines: Two honest ways to skip a destructor, on purpose.
Manually drop: the same bytes, no automatic drop. Hand the value back with into inner, and it drops.
Box leak: cut the owner, keep the bytes for the whole program.
Neither one fixes drop order. For that, reorder your declarations.
Twenty fifteen, just before Rust one point oh.
A thread API handed out a guard whose drop joined the child thread. The child borrowed the parent's stack, so the parent couldn't leave first.
Then someone forgot the guard, in safe code.
The parent's frame went away, and the child kept running, with a reference into it.
Safe code. Memory unsafety.
The fix wasn't to forbid leaks. It was to admit that destructors may never run.
So put the guarantee in a function call, not in a destructor.
Thread scope joins every thread before it returns. A return can't be forgotten.
The general rule: unsafe code must never rely on drop running.
And when you hand out a proxy, make the owner safe first. A vector sets its length to zero before it gives out a drain. Forget the drain, and you only leak more.
That's called leak amplification.
Prove it, one of three.
A function takes a parameter a, a tuple parameter with b and c, and has one local, d.
In what order do the four drop?
answer: D, c, b, a.
The local first. Then the parameters, last and in reverse... and inside the tuple pattern, c before b.

lines: Two of three.
You write let underscore equals a write lock, and then increment a counter.
Is the counter protected?
answer: The compiler refuses it.
An underscore binds nothing, so the guard would die at the semicolon and the increment would run unlocked... which is exactly why that line is a deny-by-default lint.
Name the guard.

lines: Three of three. A code review.
Someone proposes an API that hands out a guard, and says the guard must be dropped, or the device keeps writing into the buffer.
Is it sound?
answer: Unsound. A safe caller can forget the guard, the buffer is freed, and the device keeps writing.
Soundness may never depend on drop running.
Move the stop into a function that takes a closure, like thread scope.

lines: Six things to keep.
A destructor is your drop, then the fields, in order. Locals go in reverse.
A temporary dies at its semicolon, and the twenty twenty-four edition ends two of them sooner.
One owner means one release. That's RAII.
Leaking is safe. So soundness never depends on drop running.
A type with a drop keeps its fields until it dies.
Next: how do you take one field out early... say, to hand the buffer back to its pool, from inside a guard?
